entry.title: Video generation infra: bottlenecks and trade-offs

link.title: Video generation infra: bottlenecks and trade-offs

entry.content:
中文 English

LLM serving has built up a fairly mature set of intuitions: decode is bound by memory bandwidth, so batching adds throughput almost for free; speculative decoding speeds things up without changing the output distribution; the KV cache is the main consumer of memory; TTFT and TBT describe the user experience. Video generation inference looks like a similar problem — the same Transformers, the same questions of scheduling, parallelism and memory — yet these intuitions fail almost one by one.

This post records where and why they fail. Public material mostly covers the parts of papers that worked or vendors’ final designs; the ideas that look reasonable but do not work are rarely written down, and this post starts from exactly such a case: a batching attempt that gained nothing. The numbers here are of three kinds: estimates derived from public model configs, measurements on a single A100 (marked “Measured” in the figures), and a few personal observations. Each states its conditions, and none is a complete benchmark.

01 Batching 02 Acceleration 03 Quality 04 AR and streaming 05 Frameworks 06 Directions

01Batching: arithmetic intensity sets the room for batching

The original idea was to bring over LLM-style continuous batching: even though most of a DiT is compute-bound, its memory-bound operations might still gain from batching, so requests would be co-batched at denoising-step boundaries. With a 5B model and long chunks, the profile showed compute was still the bottleneck, and co-batching did not bring the expected gain.

In hindsight, this follows directly from arithmetic intensity. For a linear layer over M tokens with hidden size d, the compute is 2Md² FLOPs and the bf16 traffic is about 2(2Md + d²) bytes:

\[I = \frac{2Md^2}{2(2Md + d^2)} = \frac{Md}{2M + d}\quad \text{FLOP/byte}\]
Workload Tokens per forward pass M Intensity I
LLM decode, batch 1 1 ≈ 1
LLM decode, batch 32 32 ≈ 31
Wan 1.3B, 480p, 81 frames, batch 1 32,760 ≈ 750
Same, batch 4 131,040 ≈ 763

The LLM rows use d = 4096 and the Wan rows d = 1536; the VAE compresses 81 frames into 21 latent frames of 1,560 tokens each. An H100 SXM has about 989 TFLOPS of dense bf16 compute and about 3.35 TB/s of HBM bandwidth, so its ridge point is about 295 FLOP/byte. Only linear layers are counted, not attention or elementwise ops.

In LLM decode, going from batch 1 to 32 raises intensity about 30×, still below the ridge point, so batching pays off almost linearly. A single video DiT request is already far above the ridge point; a larger batch only pushes I toward its ceiling of d/2 = 768. From batch 1 to 4, intensity rises by only about 2%.

A larger model does not change this. For Wan2.2 TI2V 5B at 720p and 121 frames (27,280 tokens per forward pass), batch 2 still gives 1.00× the DiT throughput of batch 1; from batch 3 on, the job no longer fits on a 40 GB A100 even with the text encoder moved off the GPU. Batching does not raise throughput, and it runs into the memory limit first.

Solving I < 295 for M gives M < 295d / (d − 590): about 480 tokens at d = 1536 and about 330 at d = 5120. Linear layers return to the memory-bound regime only when a forward pass has a few hundred tokens, as in low-resolution text-to-image or very short clips.

So why doesn’t “exploiting the memory-bound operations” work either? Elementwise ops such as norms, activations and RoPE are indeed bandwidth-bound, but their intensity does not depend on batch size: batching scales their reads, writes and compute by the same factor, so the ratio stays the same. This overhead is better handled by kernel fusion than by batching.

For this kind of workload, then, scheduling is less about filling batches and more about when a request starts, which machine it runs on and how many GPUs it gets. SlackServe adjusts GPU resources, step count and resolution together under SLO constraints; TetriServe, for text-to-image, adjusts each request’s sequence-parallel degree per step; GF-DiT studies elastic parallel allocation. All three tune how many GPUs to give and how to split the work, not how many requests to merge.

02Acceleration: first ask which term it changes

\[\begin{aligned} T(G) &\approx T_{\mathrm{other}}(G) + N\,t_{\mathrm{step}}(G) \\ C &= G\,T(G) \end{aligned}\]

N is the step count and G the number of GPUs; tstep includes communication that is not hidden, and Tother collects encoding, decoding and other overhead. C is the GPU-seconds a request occupies on G GPUs.

Under this decomposition, the common techniques rank roughly as step distillation ≫ sparse attention ≈ quantization > diffusion caching > VAE optimization. The ranking rests on which term each technique changes and where its ceiling lies, not on a particular measurement; it can shift with model, resolution and length. Kernel fusion does not fit neatly into this ranking: its gain depends mainly on how much the baseline already fuses.

Step distillation changes N. Methods such as DMD2 and rCM compress 20–50 steps to about 4, and distilled models usually no longer need CFG, which saves another half of the compute. Its costs are in quality and training, not in the inference system.

Sparse attention changes only the attention part of tstep, so its gain is bounded by Amdahl’s law. If attention takes a fraction p of a step’s compute and is itself sped up s times:

\[S_{\mathrm{step}} = \frac{1}{(1-p) + p/s} \;\le\; \frac{1}{1-p}\]

Estimated by FLOPs, p is about 0.7 for Wan 1.3B at 480p and 81 frames, so even if attention vanished entirely, a step would get at most about 3.4× faster. Attention compute grows with the square of the token count, so higher resolution and longer videos raise p, and the ceiling with it.

That p is a FLOPs estimate; measured by kernel time it is lower. The figure below was measured on an A100 (bf16, the FlashAttention kernel behind PyTorch SDPA, the default diffusers implementation): attention takes about 52%, which caps the per-step speedup at about 2.1×. Another 29% goes to elementwise ops such as norms, modulation and type conversions, whose FLOPs are negligible but whose time is not.

The same measurement on Wan2.2 TI2V 5B (720p, 121 frames, d = 3072) puts attention at only about 39%, a per-step ceiling of about 1.6×: with a larger hidden size and fewer tokens, the linear layers take a larger share.

Quantization also acts on tstep. FP8 has twice the peak compute of bf16, which is the theoretical ceiling for linear layers; methods like SageAttention extend quantization to attention. The real gain depends on the kernel implementation and on how much accuracy loss is acceptable.

Diffusion caching skips part of the computation in similar adjacent steps. It relies on adjacent steps being similar; in few-step models each step changes more, so there is less to reuse and quality is harder to control.

Kernel fusion targets the elementwise ops inside each step. Their FLOPs are negligible, yet in the profile above they take about 29% of kernel time; fusing norms, modulation and type conversions into neighboring kernels directly shortens tstep. That share comes from the default diffusers implementation without torch.compile, though; in an inference framework that already fuses these ops, much less is left.

VAE optimization handles the overhead outside the steps. It is barely visible in a 50-step model, but the smaller N gets, the larger Tother’s share: after distillation, encoding, decoding and data movement can go from negligible to significant. A faster step does not mean an equally faster request, and lower latency does not mean fewer GPU-hours.

In the A100 measurement below, VAE decoding takes only about 3% of end-to-end time at 50 steps with CFG; running the same checkpoint for just 4 steps without CFG raises that to about 43% (float32 VAE, no tiling).

The VAE’s cost is not only time: activations in the decoder grow with resolution and frame count. At the 480p, 81-frame setting below, the float32 VAE decode already peaks about 6.7 GB above DiT denoising; with tiling it drops to about the DiT’s level, at the cost of decode time (not measured here).

There is one more multi-GPU reason the speedups do not multiply: sparse attention reduces compute, but if the full K/V is still sent, the compute time that Ring uses to hide communication shrinks as well. A single-GPU gain has to be re-estimated in the multi-GPU setting.

Try step count, GPU count and communication overheadOpen calculator

An analytical estimate for seeing trends; the defaults are not calibrated against measurements.

03Quality: a harder constraint than speed

In LLM inference, one of the most influential speedups is lossless: speculative decoding guarantees the output distribution does not change. In video generation, the speedups with large gains — distillation, sparsity, quantization, caching — are almost all lossy. Quality evaluation also lacks a cheap, reliable metric like accuracy, so every speedup carries an extra evaluation cost.

Parallelism can change the result too. Different sequence-parallel splits, reduction orders and attention backends give different floating-point results; denoising can amplify those initial differences, so multi-GPU and single-GPU outputs may not look the same. Where reproducibility or A/B comparison matters, check this beforehand.

Length is limited by the training distribution. A bidirectional model’s usable length is usually close to its training length; beyond that, repetition or structural collapse is common. Simply extending the sequence means extrapolating positional encodings, which the inference system cannot solve on its own.

Changing the inference pipeline is riskier than it looks. Injecting the previous segment’s K/V into a bidirectional model, or adding an extra fusion module, both seem to carry information across segments; in my own attempts, though, the first thing such changes brought was unstable image quality. Possible causes include misaligned positional encodings and a train–inference mismatch, which I have not yet isolated one by one. Getting information in does not mean the model uses it as intended.

By contrast, video models are very sensitive to text conditioning. Without retraining, fuller and more consistent text descriptions may help cross-segment consistency more than changing the inference pipeline. This is the choice I made after experimenting so far, not a general conclusion.

04AR: fast is not enough, it has to keep up with playback

Causal generators such as CausVid and Self Forcing let video be produced segment by segment. Serving metrics map onto LLM ones: the wait for the first segment resembles TTFT, and the gap between segments resembles TBT. The difference is the playback buffer: as long as the next segment finishes before the buffer runs out, the gap itself is invisible to the user. The same generation speed can feel completely different depending on the buffer margin.

SlackServe organizes resource allocation around exactly this remaining playable time. Serving goals closer to the user experience are therefore time to the first segment, playback stalls and control responsiveness, plus how many streams can be served under these constraints.

Autoregression also brings the KV cache back to video generation. History KV directly consumes the memory budget that streams share; for bf16 standard multi-head attention:

\[M_{\mathrm{KV}} = 4 L d\,n_{\mathrm{history}}\quad\text{bytes}\]

Most current AR video models attend only within a local window; LongLive also keeps the first frame as a sink, the same idea as StreamingLLM. The window itself is the simplest form of KV compression: it caps each stream’s memory, at the cost of forgetting whatever falls outside it.

Since 2026, finer-grained KV compression has appeared on the generation side: Quant VideoGen quantizes the KV to 2 bits, and DensityKV and FrameFold select or merge history KV under a fixed budget. Video understanding started earlier: work such as InfiniPot-V compresses the KV of visual tokens in streaming video QA.

The two problems are not the same. On the understanding side, compression saves memory; the KV is only read by the question, and tokens can be selected based on it. On the generation side, the window already bounds memory, so compression is more about remembering a longer history within the same budget; and every compression error is reused as a condition for all later chunks and all denoising steps, where it may accumulate into drift segment after segment. Importance-based selection heuristics from the understanding side may therefore not carry over directly.

History length, the number of streams that fit and generation quality need to be weighed as one serving problem. This is one of the directions I consider most worth investing in.

05Frameworks: parallel libraries and serving systems

The following is based on the open-source code as of late October 2026. These projects move quickly, and details may have changed.

  • xDiT is a single-request parallel inference library: USP (a combination of Ulysses and Ring), PipeFusion and CFG parallelism, wrapping diffusers pipelines. It answers how one request is split across GPUs, not how multiple requests are scheduled. The parallel-state code in both SGLang Diffusion and vLLM-Omni traces back to it.
  • SGLang Diffusion adds a serving layer on top of similar parallelism: combinations of CFG, TP and sequence parallelism, encoding, denoising and decoding that can be deployed separately, several attention backends, and dynamic batching for some models (such as Wan2.1). It also groups acceleration options into exact, lossless and high tiers by their effect on the output, which ties directly to Section 03.
  • vLLM-Omni targets omni-modal models. Its diffusion part runs either per request or per step; per-step execution currently covers only a few video models, one request at a time. What sets it apart is KV transfer between an AR model and a DiT, aimed at models that combine an LLM with diffusion.

Given Section 01, the value of batching and step-level scheduling in these two serving frameworks may lie mostly outside video throughput: image and low-resolution requests are still in the range where batching works; step-level execution gives a hook for preemption, interleaving and resource adjustment; and a unified request interface makes it easier to share infrastructure with LLM serving. For high-resolution video requests, batching itself is most likely not where the gains come from.

06Directions worth watching

Not every direction leaves room for infra, but the following ones change the problems an inference system has to solve:

  • AR-DiT and long video. Breaking the training-length limit brings back the KV cache, and with it the serving problems of Section 04.
  • Linear and hybrid attention. Work such as SANA-Video and Video DeltaNet lowers the cost of long sequences; few open video models use it yet, so system-level optimization still lacks a target.
  • Agentic generation. An LLM plans the shots, a VLM judges quality, and a video model generates. Candidates can share text encoding and be pruned early with cheap previews; the unit of scheduling shifts from a single request to a workflow graph.
  • 3D memory and procedural scenes. Editing an explicit scene representation makes consistency easier to guarantee; the video model moves closer to a renderer, and what the inference system must provide changes with it.

Looking back, video generation inference shares many components with LLM inference, but the bottleneck sits elsewhere: in compute, not bandwidth; in resource allocation, not batching; in quality constraints, not lossless speedups. Before carrying an LLM serving method over, first check that the assumption it relies on still holds.

October 2026. Personal observations are limited to the stated settings; quality comparisons are still to come. Schematics, intensities and capacities are estimates from public configs; figures marked "Measured" come from a single A100, with the setup in each caption.
entry.summary: LLM-serving intuitions fail one by one on video generation — batching, acceleration, quality and streaming.

entry.title: 视频生成 infra：瓶颈与取舍

link.title: 视频生成 infra：瓶颈与取舍

entry.content:
中文 English

LLM serving 已经积累了一套相对成熟的直觉：decode 受内存带宽限制，合批几乎可以白赚吞吐；speculative decoding 能在不改变输出分布的前提下加速；KV cache 是显存的主要占用；TTFT 与 TBT 刻画用户体验。视频生成推理看起来是相近的问题——同样是 Transformer，同样涉及调度、并行与显存管理——但上面这几条直觉几乎逐条失效。

本文记录这些直觉在哪里失效、为什么失效。公开材料大多是论文的成功部分或厂商的最终方案，“看起来合理却走不通”的那一层很少被写下来，而本文的起点正是一次没有收益的 batching 尝试。文中的数字分三类：按公开模型配置推得的估算、单张 A100 上的实测（图中标为“实测”），以及少量个人观察；均注明条件，都不是完整的 benchmark。

01 Batching 02 加速 03 质量 04 AR 与流式 05 框架 06 方向

01Batching：算术强度决定合批空间

最初的设想是把 LLM 的 continuous batching 搬过来：即使 DiT 的主体是 compute-bound，其中的 memory-bound 操作或许仍能从合批中获益，于是按 denoising step 的边界做 co-batch。在 5B 模型、长 chunk 的配置下，profile 显示瓶颈仍是计算，co-batch 也没有带来预期收益。

事后看，这个结果可以从算术强度直接推出。对 M 个 token、隐藏维度 d 的线性层，计算量为 2Md²，bf16 下的读写量约为 2(2Md + d²) 字节：

\[I = \frac{2Md^2}{2(2Md + d^2)} = \frac{Md}{2M + d}\quad \text{FLOP/byte}\]
负载 每次前向的 token 数 M 强度 I
LLM decode，batch 1 1 ≈ 1
LLM decode，batch 32 32 ≈ 31
Wan 1.3B，480p、81 帧，batch 1 32,760 ≈ 750
同上，batch 4 131,040 ≈ 763

LLM 行取 d = 4096，Wan 行取 d = 1536；81 帧经 VAE 压缩为 21 个 latent 帧，每帧 1,560 token。H100 SXM 的 bf16 稠密算力约 989 TFLOPS、HBM 带宽约 3.35 TB/s，拐点约 295 FLOP/byte。只计线性层，不含 attention 与逐元素算子。

LLM decode 中，batch 从 1 增至 32，强度提高约 30 倍，仍在拐点以下，合批的收益几乎线性。视频 DiT 的单个请求已经远超拐点，batch 再大也只是把 I 推向 d/2 = 768 的上限：从 batch 1 到 4，强度只提高约 2%。

换成更大的模型，结论不变：Wan2.2 TI2V 5B 在 720p、121 帧下（每次前向 27,280 token），batch 2 的 DiT 吞吐仍是 batch 1 的 1.00 倍；batch 3 起，即使把文本编码器移出显存，40 GB 的 A100 也放不下。合批不仅不提高吞吐，还会先撞上显存上限。

反过来解 I < 295，得到 M < 295d / (d − 590)：d = 1536 时约 480 token，d = 5120 时约 330 token。只有单次前向的 token 数降到几百量级，线性层才回到 memory-bound 区间，例如低分辨率的文生图，或非常短的片段。

那么“利用其中的 memory-bound 操作”为什么也不成立？norm、激活、RoPE 这类逐元素算子确实受带宽限制，但它们的强度与 batch 无关：合批只是把读写和计算按同样倍数放大，比例不变。这类开销更适合用 kernel fusion 处理，而不是合批。

因此，这类负载的调度重心不在“凑 batch”，而在何时启动、放在哪台机器、分配多少 GPU。SlackServe 在 SLO 约束下同时调整 GPU 资源、步数与分辨率；TetriServe 面向文生图，按 step 调整每个请求的序列并行度；GF-DiT 研究弹性的并行分配。三者调的都是“给多少卡、怎么切”，而不是“合多少请求”。

02加速：先看它改变哪一项

\[\begin{aligned} T(G) &\approx T_{\mathrm{other}}(G) + N\,t_{\mathrm{step}}(G) \\ C &= G\,T(G) \end{aligned}\]

N 为步数，G 为 GPU 数；tstep 含未被隐藏的通信，Tother 汇总编码、解码等开销。C 为请求占用 G 张卡期间的 GPU-seconds。

按这个分解，常见手段的收益大致可以排序为：步数蒸馏 ≫ 稀疏 attention ≈ 量化 > diffusion cache > VAE 优化。排序依据是每种手段能改变哪一项、上限在哪里，而不是某组具体实测；模型、分辨率与时长不同，排序可能变化。kernel fusion 不容易放进这个排序：它的收益主要取决于基线实现已经融合了多少。

步数蒸馏改变 N。 DMD2、rCM 等方法可将 20–50 步压缩到 4 步左右，蒸馏后的模型通常也不再需要 CFG，等于再省去一半计算。它的代价在质量和训练成本上，而不在推理系统里。

稀疏 attention 只改变 tstep 中 attention 的部分，收益受 Amdahl 定律约束。设 attention 占单步计算的比例为 p、自身加速 s 倍：

\[S_{\mathrm{step}} = \frac{1}{(1-p) + p/s} \;\le\; \frac{1}{1-p}\]

按 FLOPs 估算，Wan 1.3B 在 480p、81 帧下 p 约为 0.7，即使 attention 完全消失，单步加速也不超过约 3.4×。attention 的计算随 token 数平方增长，分辨率与时长越大，p 越高，上限随之提高。

上面的 p 是按 FLOPs 估算的，按 kernel 时间算会更低。下图在 A100 上实测（bf16，PyTorch SDPA 的 FlashAttention 内核，diffusers 默认实现）：attention 约占 52%，对应的单步上限约 2.1×；另有约 29% 落在 norm、调制、类型转换等逐元素算子上，这些算子的 FLOPs 可以忽略，时间却不能。

同样的测量换到 Wan2.2 TI2V 5B（720p、121 帧，d = 3072）上，attention 只占约 39%，单步上限约 1.6×：隐藏维度更大、token 数更少时，线性层的份额随之上升。

量化同样作用于 tstep。 FP8 相对 bf16 的峰值算力为 2 倍，这是线性层的理论上限；SageAttention 一类方法把量化延伸到 attention。实际收益取决于 kernel 实现与可接受的精度损失。

diffusion cache 跳过相邻相似步的部分计算。它依赖相邻步之间的相似性；少步模型中每一步的变化更大，可复用的空间相应缩小，质量也更难控制。

kernel fusion 作用于单步之内的逐元素算子。 这些算子的 FLOPs 可以忽略，在前面的 profile 图里却占了约 29% 的 kernel 时间；把 norm、调制、类型转换融进相邻的 kernel，能直接缩短 tstep。不过这个比例来自 diffusers 的默认实现，没有开 torch.compile；在已经做过融合的推理框架里，剩下的空间会小得多。

VAE 优化处理的是单步之外的开销。 它在 50 步的模型上不显眼，但 N 越小，Tother 的占比越高：蒸馏之后，编码、解码与数据搬运可能从可以忽略变为不可忽略。单步快，不等于端到端同样快；延迟低，也不等于用卡更省。

下图的 A100 实测中，50 步、带 CFG 时 VAE 解码只占端到端时间的约 3%；同一 checkpoint 只跑 4 步、关闭 CFG 时，这一比例升至约 43%（VAE 为 float32、未开 tiling）。

VAE 的开销不只体现在时间上：解码阶段的激活随分辨率和帧数增长。在下图的 480p、81 帧配置下，float32 VAE 解码的显存峰值已经比 DiT 去噪高约 6.7 GB；开启 tiling 后降到与 DiT 相当，代价是解码时间（这里未测）。

各项加速比不能直接相乘，还有一个多卡上的原因：稀疏 attention 减少了计算，若仍传完整的 K/V，Ring 用来覆盖通信的计算时间也会缩短。单卡收益需要放回多卡配置中重新估算。

试算步数、GPU 数与通信开销展开计算器

解析估算，用于看趋势；默认参数未经实测校准。

03质量：比速度更硬的约束

LLM 推理中，最有影响力的加速之一是无损的：speculative decoding 可以保证输出分布不变。视频生成中，收益较大的加速——蒸馏、稀疏、量化、cache——几乎都是有损的。质量评估本身也缺少像准确率那样廉价、可靠的指标，这使得每一项加速都需要额外的评估成本。

并行也可能改变结果。 序列并行的切分方式、规约顺序、attention backend 不同，浮点结果就会不同；去噪过程可能放大这些初始差异，多卡与单卡的输出在视觉上未必一致。对需要复现或做 A/B 对比的场景，这一点需要事先确认。

时长受训练分布限制。 双向模型的可用时长通常接近训练时长，超出后容易出现重复或结构崩坏。直接拉长序列涉及位置编码的外推，并不是推理系统能单独解决的问题。

改动推理流程的风险，大于看上去的程度。 往双向模型注入上一段的 K/V、增加额外的融合模块，看起来都能补上跨段信息；但在个人的尝试中，这类改动首先带来的是画质不稳定。可能的原因包括位置编码错位与训练–推理不一致，这两点尚未逐一隔离验证。信息传进去了，不代表模型能按预期使用它。

与之相对，视频模型对文本条件非常敏感。在不重新训练的前提下，更完整、更一致的文本描述，可能比修改推理流程更有助于跨段一致性。这是现阶段实验后的选择，还不是通用结论。

04AR：算得快，还要赶上播放

CausVid、Self Forcing 等因果生成模型让视频可以逐段输出。服务指标可以和 LLM 类比：首段等待近似 TTFT，段间间隔近似 TBT。区别在于播放缓冲：只要下一段在缓冲耗尽前完成，段间间隔本身对用户不可见。同样的生成速度，面对不同的缓冲余量，体验可能完全不同。

SlackServe 正是用剩余可播放时间组织资源分配。更贴近用户体验的服务目标因此是：首段等待、播放卡顿、控制响应，以及在这些约束下能承载多少条流。

自回归也让 KV cache 回到了视频生成中。历史 KV 直接占用多流共享的显存预算，按 bf16 普通多头 attention 估算：

\[M_{\mathrm{KV}} = 4 L d\,n_{\mathrm{history}}\quad\text{bytes}\]

目前主流的 AR 视频模型大多只在局部窗口内做 attention；LongLive 额外保留首帧作为 sink，思路与 StreamingLLM 一致。窗口本身就是最简单的 KV 压缩：它给每条流的显存设了上限，代价是窗口之外的内容被遗忘。

2026 年起，生成侧开始出现更细的 KV 压缩：Quant VideoGen 将 KV 量化到 2 bit，DensityKV 与 FrameFold 在固定预算下筛选或合并历史 KV。视频理解侧更早开始做这件事，InfiniPot-V 等工作在流式视频问答中压缩视觉 token 的 KV。

两边的问题并不相同。理解侧压缩是为了省显存，KV 只被问题读取，还可以按问题挑选 token。生成侧的窗口已经限住了显存，压缩更多是为了在同等预算下记住更远的历史；而每一次压缩误差，都会作为后续所有 chunk、所有去噪步的条件被反复使用，并可能逐段累积为漂移。理解侧基于重要性的筛选启发式，因此未必能直接迁移到生成侧。

history 长度、可容纳流数与生成质量，需要作为同一个服务问题来权衡。这是本文认为最值得投入的方向之一。

05框架：并行库与服务系统

以下基于 2026 年 10 月底的开源代码，各项目迭代很快，细节可能已经变化。

  • xDiT 是单请求的并行推理库：USP（Ulysses 与 Ring 的组合）、PipeFusion、CFG 并行，封装 diffusers 的管线。它回答“一个请求如何切到多张卡上”，不负责多请求调度。SGLang Diffusion 与 vLLM-Omni 的并行状态管理代码都可以追溯到它。
  • SGLang Diffusion 在类似的并行能力之上加了服务层：CFG、TP 与序列并行的组合，编码、去噪、解码可以分离部署，支持多种 attention backend，并对部分模型（如 Wan2.1）提供动态合批。它还按 exact、lossless、high 三档区分加速选项对输出的影响，这与第 03 节的问题直接相关。
  • vLLM-Omni 以全模态模型为目标，扩散部分有请求级与 step 级两种执行方式；step 级执行在视频模型上目前只覆盖少数几个，且为单请求。它的特色在于 AR 模型与 DiT 之间的 KV 传递，面向的是“LLM + 扩散”组合的模型。

结合第 01 节，这两个服务框架做合批与 step 级调度，价值可能主要不在提高视频请求的吞吐：图像或低分辨率请求仍处在合批有效的区间；step 粒度的执行为抢占、交错与资源调整提供了切入点；统一的请求接口也便于和 LLM 服务共用基础设施。对高分辨率视频请求，合批本身大概率不是收益来源。

06值得关注的方向

并非每个方向都有 infra 的空间，但以下几个方向会改变推理系统要解决的问题：

  • AR-DiT 与长视频。 突破训练时长的限制，KV cache 随之回归，第 04 节的服务问题随之出现。
  • 线性注意力与混合注意力。 SANA-Video、Video DeltaNet 等工作降低长序列的成本；目前开源的视频模型仍少，系统层面的优化还缺少落地对象。
  • Agentic 生成。 LLM 规划分镜，VLM 评估质量，视频模型执行生成。多个候选可以共享文本编码，并借低成本预览提前淘汰，调度对象从单个请求变为一张工作流图。
  • 3D 记忆与程序化场景。 在显式场景表示上编辑更容易保证一致性，视频模型的角色趋近渲染器，对推理系统的要求也会随之改变。

回头看，视频生成推理与 LLM 推理共享许多组件，但瓶颈的位置不同：它不在带宽，而在计算；不在合批，而在资源分配；不在无损加速，而在质量约束。把 LLM serving 的方法直接搬过来之前，先确认它依赖的那条假设是否仍然成立。

2026 年 10 月。个人观察限于所述配置；画质对照待补。示意图、强度与容量为按公开配置的估算；标有“实测”的图来自单张 A100，配置见各图图注。
